title: Least squares through QR
prompt:
Fit least squares the stable way.

1. Write `back_substitute(R, b)`, which solves `R x = b` for an upper-triangular `R` with a nonzero diagonal. Start from the last row, which has one unknown, and work upwards. A loop over the rows is fine.
2. Write `lstsq_qr(X, y)`, which returns the `w` minimizing ‖Xw − y‖, using `np.linalg.qr` and your `back_substitute`.

Don't use `np.linalg.solve`, `lstsq`, `inv` or `pinv`, and never form `X.T @ X`.
hints: With X = QR, the fit Xw = Q(Rw) lives in the column space of Q. What does multiplying by Qᵀ do to the length of a vector in that space?

Q has orthonormal columns, so minimizing ‖QRw − y‖ comes down to making Rw equal Qᵀy: an upper-triangular system. Row k of R x = b reads R[k, k]·x[k] + R[k, k+1:] @ x[k+1:] = b[k], and x[k+1:] is already known when you go from the bottom up.
back_substitute: x = np.zeros(n); for k in range(n - 1, -1, -1): x[k] = (b[k] - R[k, k+1:] @ x[k+1:]) / R[k, k]. lstsq_qr: Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X); return back_substitute(R, Q.T @ y).

misconceptions.normal-equations-square-kappa: Forming XᵀX squares the condition number, so the normal equations lose twice as many digits as QR. A fit with κ(X) = 10⁷ keeps about 9 digits through QR and 2 or 3 through XᵀX.
